Global Industrial Dynamics Corp. - Q3 2023 Earnings Call Transcript

Operator:
Good morning, and welcome to the Global Industrial Dynamics Corp. Q3 2023 Earnings Conference Call. All participants are in listen-only mode. After the presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. To ask a question, you will need to request the floor through the conference system. As a reminder, this conference is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the call over to Sarah Thompson, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Thompson (Head of Investor Relations):
Thank you, Operator. Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us today to discuss Global Industrial Dynamics Corp.'s results for the third quarter. Joining me on today's call are Mark Reynolds, Chief Executive Officer; Lisa Chen, Chief Financial Officer; and David Patel, Chief Operating Officer.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that some of the statements we will be making today are forward-looking in nature and subject to certain risks and uncertainties. Please refer to our SEC filings for a complete discussion of these risks.

Now, I'd like to turn the call over to Mark Reynolds.

Mark Reynolds (CEO):
Thank you, Sarah, and good morning, everyone. I'm pleased to report on Global Industrial Dynamics Corp.'s performance for the third quarter. We've made significant progress on several fronts, delivering robust revenue growth amid resilient demand in our core end markets of construction, mining, agriculture, and manufacturing. We've seen strong order intake across these segments, with book-to-bill ratios well above 1.0x, building our backlog to record levels and providing excellent visibility. Our aftermarket parts and services business continues to accelerate, contributing an even larger share of high-margin revenue and underscoring the durability of our model. Operating margins expanded meaningfully thanks to pricing discipline and supply chain efficiencies, and we've executed aggressively on our share repurchase program to drive shareholder value. We're confident that these strategic initiatives—rooted in operational excellence, digital transformation, and exposure to secular tailwinds like infrastructure spending and electrification—are positioning us for long-term sustainable growth.

Now, I'll turn the call over to Lisa to provide more detail on our financial results.

Lisa Chen (CFO):
Thank you, Mark. Turning to our financial performance, Global Industrial Dynamics Corp. reported $2.85 billion in revenue for the third quarter, representing a 12% increase year-over-year. Gross margin expanded to 42.5%, driven by favorable product mix, pricing actions, and lower input costs. Operating expenses were $480 million, resulting in an operating income of $510 million. Our net income for the quarter was $380 million, or $2.15 per share.

We are reaffirming our guidance for the full year, with expected revenue growth of 11-13% and EPS of $8.50 to $8.80. We are committed to returning capital to shareholders through our ongoing dividends and share repurchase program.

As Mark highlighted earlier, we delivered another strong quarter driven by robust demand in our core segments: material handling equipment, CNC machining centers, and fluid power systems. Our adjusted operating margin came in at 17.8%—a 140 basis point expansion from Q3 2022—reflecting the benefits of our disciplined pricing strategy, supply chain optimizations, and a favorable product mix shift toward higher-margin aftermarket parts and services, which now represent 28% of total revenue.

Now, turning to guidance. For the fourth quarter of 2023, we are guiding adjusted operating margin to the range of 19.0% to 20.0%. This represents sequential expansion of 120 to 220 basis points from Q3 and would mark our strongest quarterly margin performance in over five years. For the full fiscal year 2023, we now expect adjusted operating margins of 18.5% to 19.0%, up from our prior guide of 17.5% to 18.5%, putting us on track for approximately 250 basis points of year-over-year expansion.

Let me unpack the key drivers behind this outlook, starting with the tailwinds. First, pricing discipline remains a cornerstone. We've successfully implemented mid-single-digit price increases across 85% of our portfolio—particularly on high-volume products like our GIDC-5000 series hydraulic pumps and next-gen RoboForge CNC lathes—with customer acceptance holding firm above 95% due to our value-based selling approach. This has added roughly 300 basis points to margins year-to-date, outpacing peers like Caterpillar and Ingersoll Rand, who reported similar but slightly lower capture rates in their recent prints.

Second, supply chain normalization and cost productivity initiatives are accelerating. Steel and aluminum input costs, which peaked at 25% above pre-pandemic levels in 2022, have now moderated by 15% sequentially, thanks to long-term offtake agreements with suppliers like Nucor and Alcoa. Our just-in-time inventory model, enhanced by SAP S/4HANA ERP integration, has reduced working capital days to 72 from 85 a year ago, freeing up $150 million in cash while boosting factory utilization to 92% across our 12 global plants. We're also realizing $80 million in annualized savings from our 'ForgeForward' lean manufacturing program, which includes AI-driven predictive maintenance on our assembly lines—reducing unplanned downtime by 22% and mirroring efficiency gains we've seen at Cummins in their engine plants.

Regionally, North America continues to outperform, contributing 55% of Q4 revenue with expected margins north of 21%. This is fueled by the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (IIJA) tailwinds, where our earthmoving equipment backlog stands at a record $4.2 billion—up 18% year-over-year—with book-to-bill at 1.4x. Data center construction boom is driving demand for our precision cooling systems, akin to trends boosting Trane Technologies. In EMEA, margins should hit 18-19%, supported by reshoring trends and EU Green Deal subsidies for energy-efficient compressors.

On the flip side, Asia-Pacific introduces some mix pressure, tempering full-year margins at the low end of our guide. China, at 20% of revenue, faces headwinds from the ongoing real estate slowdown and softening industrial capex—our book-to-bill there dipped to 0.9x in Q3. However, we're offsetting this with 25% growth in India and Southeast Asia, where localization efforts at our new Pune facility are yielding 500 basis points of margin accretion through tariff avoidance and reduced ocean freight costs. Emerging market aftermarket penetration is key here, targeting 35% of regional revenue by year-end via our DynoGuard IoT telematics platform, which has driven 40% attach rates on new equipment sales.

Strategically, we're leaning into Industry 4.0 and digital transformation to sustain this trajectory. Our $250 million CapEx plan for FY24—focused on expanding capacity at our Rockford, IL automation campus—will support a shift to software-enabled products, where margins exceed 30%. We've already seen this in our SmartForge suite, with embedded edge computing boosting service recurring revenue by 35% YoY. Full-year SG&A as a percent of sales is expected to delever to 9.5% from 10.2%, driven by zero-based budgeting and headcount optimization—we're right-sizing non-core functions while investing in high-ROI R&D like hydrogen-compatible fluid power systems for the energy transition.

Of course, no guidance is without risks. We continue to monitor inflation—labor costs up 4.5% in bargaining units—geopolitical tensions impacting Ukraine-sourced titanium, and FX headwinds from a stronger USD, which could shave 50 basis points off margins if the dollar appreciates another 5%. That said, our $3.8 billion backlog provides strong visibility, with 70% of Q4 revenue already booked.

Before I dive deeper into segments, let me highlight a key bright spot in our P&L: our aftermarket parts and services business, which continues to be the high-margin engine driving sustainable profitability and resilience in our portfolio. As you know, in the industrial equipment sector—where we design and manufacture mission-critical assets like our flagship TitanPress hydraulic forging presses, RoboForge CNC machining centers, and ServoBot industrial automation systems—aftermarket revenue is the gift that keeps on giving. These revenues stem from OEM replacement parts, field service contracts, remanufacturing programs, and our growing suite of digital services, all supporting an installed base of over 150,000 machines worldwide with average lifecycles exceeding 20 years.

In Q3, aftermarket parts and services revenue accelerated to $728 million, up 18% year-over-year and 9% sequentially from Q2. This marks the 11th consecutive quarter of double-digit growth, outpacing our new equipment sales by a wide margin. As a percentage of total revenue, aftermarket now contributes 36%—an all-time high, expanding 400 basis points from 32% in the prior-year period and up from 28% two years ago. For context, this compares favorably to peers like Ingersoll Rand, which reported around 33% aftermarket mix last quarter, and Caterpillar's 32% in their latest machinery segment update. Our total revenue for the quarter came in at $2.85 billion, so this segment alone added over $100 million in incremental top-line growth versus last year.

What’s fueling this momentum? First, organic drivers tied to end-market dynamics. Global industrial capex utilization rates have rebounded to 82%—per recent ISM data—boosting machine runtime and parts wear. Our customers in automotive, aerospace, and heavy truck OEMs, facing persistent supply chain bottlenecks for new equipment, are extending the life of existing assets. This is evident in our parts revenue, which grew 22% YoY to $450 million, led by high-demand consumables like hydraulic seals, carbide tooling inserts, and precision servo motors. Service revenue, including planned maintenance and uptime contracts, rose 14% to $278 million, reflecting stronger attachment rates on our newer ServoBot lines, where service penetration now exceeds 65%.

Second, technical initiatives are supercharging adoption. The rollout of our TitanConnect IoT platform—our edge-to-cloud ecosystem with over 50,000 connected assets—has been a game-changer. It leverages machine learning for predictive maintenance, reducing unplanned downtime by an average of 28% for enrolled customers, per our internal telemetry data. Adoption hit 27% of our eligible installed base this quarter, up from 18% a year ago, driving a 35% surge in digital service upsells like remote diagnostics and AI-optimized parts forecasting. We’re also scaling our RemanForge program, where we refurbish cores into like-new components at 40-60% cost savings versus new parts—think rebuilding a 500-ton TitanPress ram assembly. This generated $85 million in Q3, with EBITDA margins north of 55%, and positions us ahead of competitors like Siemens in circular economy plays.

Regionally, performance was robust across the board but with bright spots. North America, our largest market at 45% of aftermarket revenue, grew 25% YoY to $328 million, propelled by the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act’s $1.2 trillion spend. Onshoring trends in EV battery gigafactories—customers like Tesla and GM expanding domestic forging capacity—have spiked demand for our RoboForge upgrades. EMEA delivered steady 12% growth to $210 million, despite softer German auto output; our service network expansion into Poland and Turkey, adding 15 new depots, helped capture aftermarket share from independents. APAC was the star, up 22% to $190 million, fueled by China’s semiconductor reshoring and India’s 'Make in India' push for CNC equipment. We’re seeing particular strength in high-precision parts for semiconductor fab tools, mirroring trends at Applied Materials.

Strategically, we’re laser-focused on margin expansion and mix shift. Aftermarket delivered 48% EBITDA margins in Q3—nearly double our 25% for new equipment—contributing over 60% to segment profit despite representing just 36% of revenue. Our book-to-bill ratio here stands at 1.25x, signaling a multi-year runway. Looking ahead, we’re targeting 40%+ aftermarket contribution by 2025 through three levers: (1) M&A tuck-ins, like our recent $150 million acquisition of ForgeTech Services, adding 2,000 field techs and boosting North American density; (2) digital twin integrations across our portfolio, partnering with NVIDIA for GPU-accelerated simulations to preempt failures; and (3) outcome-based contracts, where we guarantee 98% uptime for premiums—piloted with Ford’s F-150 Lightning line, already converting 20% of spot service to annuities.

As we dive into the details, I'd like to focus on our order intake and book-to-bill dynamics, broken out by key end markets. This remains a critical leading indicator for our visibility into future revenue, especially in our cyclical industrial equipment business. Overall, Q3 order intake came in at $2.8 billion, up 12% year-over-year and 5% sequentially from Q2. This reflects robust demand across most segments, driven by infrastructure tailwinds, commodity price stabilization, and our ongoing share gains from new product ramps.

Our trailing 12-month book-to-bill ratio stands at 1.18x, with a quarterly ratio of 1.22x—well above the 1.0x breakeven that supports backlog growth. Ending backlog now sits at a record $12.4 billion, up 18% YoY, providing strong multi-quarter visibility. Lead times for core products like our 300-ton-class mining haul trucks and 50-ton excavators remain extended at 9-12 months, reflecting capacity constraints we're addressing through our $450 million CapEx plan this year, including expansions at our Peoria and Belo Horizonte facilities.

Let me break this down by end market, starting with construction, which represented 42% of Q3 bookings. Order intake here surged 22% YoY to $1.18 billion, fueled by unprecedented infrastructure spending globally. In North America, which accounted for 55% of our construction bookings, intake rose 28% YoY, thanks to the IIJA's $1.2 trillion pipeline accelerating projects like highway expansions and data center builds. Our book-to-bill hit 1.35x, with standout performance from our NextGen hydraulic excavators, like the 374 model with 15% better fuel efficiency via our HydroMax system. We're gaining share from Komatsu in the 40-60 ton class, where we've captured 3 points of market share YTD per IronPlanet data.

EMEA was softer at +8% YoY growth, pressured by high interest rates delaying OEM capex, but APAC offset this with 35% growth, led by India's $130 billion infra budget boosting demand for wheel loaders and dozers. LATAM grew 15%, anchored by Brazil's port expansions. Strategically, we're leaning into digital twins and telematics integration—our SiteConnect platform now has 250,000 connected assets—driving 20% higher repeat orders from fleet managers optimizing utilization.

Mining bookings were resilient at $850 million, up 9% YoY and flat sequentially, comprising 30% of total intake. Book-to-bill came in at 1.15x, supported by a $10.5 billion backlog that's up 25% YoY. Copper and iron ore prices holding above $4/lb and $100/ton, respectively, have sustained capex appetites despite gold's volatility. North America led with 18% growth, driven by Nevada Gold Mines' fleet renewals favoring our 793F autonomous-ready haul trucks, where we've logged over 1 million autonomous hours cumulatively.

Australia, 40% of our mining mix, grew 12% on Rio Tinto and BHP expansions, though lead times stretched to 14 months amid battery-electric transition delays. We're ahead of the curve here with our e-785 electric shovel pilot, delivering 30% OPEX savings in trials with Fortescue. China was flat due to property sector spillovers curbing coal demand, but we're mitigating via aftermarket upticks—service contracts now 35% of mining revenue. Insight: We're targeting 5% share gain in battery-electric mining equipment by 2025 through JVs with ABB, capitalizing on ESG mandates from funds like BlackRock.

Ag equipment orders totaled $420 million, up 5% YoY but down 3% sequentially, or 15% of total bookings. Book-to-bill dipped to 1.05x, reflecting weather headwinds and farmer balance sheet caution post-2023's high input costs. North America, 60% of ag mix, was up 8% on strong corn/soy yields boosting combine and tractor demand—our 8R series precision ag tractors with AutoTrac vision saw 25% order growth. We're benchmarking well against Deere, with 2 points of share gain in high-horsepower segments per AEM data.

EMEA grew 12% on EU subsidies for sustainable farming, where our electric compact tractors are ramping. APAC disappointed at -2% due to China's oversupply and India's monsoon delays, but LATAM surged 20% on Brazil's soybean boom. Strategically, we're investing $200 million in autonomy, with beta tests of our Hands-Free Farming system on 7,000+ acre operations yielding 15% labor savings—key to countering Deere's dominance and addressing rural labor shortages.

Quickly, power generation and oil & gas rounded out at 13% of bookings, with $360 million intake up 10% YoY. Book-to-bill 1.12x, driven by LNG export ramps in the US Gulf Coast for our gas turbine gensets, and Middle East Aramco projects for drilling rigs.

I'll now turn to our demand trends across our core end markets—construction, mining, agriculture, and manufacturing—which collectively represent about 85% of our backlog and drove 12% organic revenue growth in Q3. Overall, we're seeing resilient demand underpinned by multi-year capex cycles, though headwinds from elevated interest rates and softening commodity prices in select areas are tempering near-term visibility. Our order intake rose 9% year-over-year to $2.8 billion, with backlog now at a record $18.5 billion, up 15% sequentially, signaling strong forward visibility into 2025.

Construction (42% of Q3 revenue, up 14% YoY): Demand remains robust, fueled by global infrastructure megatrends and pent-up non-residential spending. In North America, which accounts for 55% of our construction orders, U.S. highway and bridge projects under the IIJA are accelerating—highway contract awards hit $52 billion YTD, per ARTBA data—driving 18% YoY growth in our large excavators and wheel loaders, like our 390-ton-class models with hybrid powertrains. Housing starts are stabilizing at 1.4 million annualized, supporting compact equipment demand, though multifamily softness is capping residential exposure.

EMEA saw 10% growth, bolstered by EU Green Deal-funded rail and data center builds, where our electric mini-excavators gained 25% market share in Germany per VDMA stats. Asia-Pacific, however, moderated to 5% growth amid China's property sector deleveraging—urban renewal projects are offsetting this, with our compact track loaders up 12% in Southeast Asia. Strategically, we're leaning into sustainability: 30% of new construction orders feature telematics-enabled machines with Grade with Control tech, reducing fuel burn by 15% and boosting fleet utilization for customers like Vinci and Bechtel. We've initiated a $150 million capacity ramp at our U.S. skid-steer plant to capture reshoring tailwinds.

Mining (28% of Q3 revenue, up 8% YoY): Here, demand is bifurcated—strong in bulk commodities, challenged in precious metals. Copper and iron ore prices, hovering at $4.20/lb and $105/tonne respectively, are driving underground and surface fleet modernizations, with our 793F haul trucks and Cat 6090 excavators logging 22% order growth globally. Autonomous haulage, now in 15% of new mining contracts, is a key driver; our Command for Hauling system, integrated with MineStar Edge, delivered 20% productivity gains at Rio Tinto's Pilbara operations last quarter.

Regionally, Australia and Latin America (55% of mining backlog) surged 16% on ESG-driven fleet electrification—our battery-electric R2900 XE loaders are 40% of orders there, aligning with BHP's net-zero goals. North America grew 6%, tempered by U.S. coal slowdowns, while Africa held flat amid permitting delays in Zambia. Insight: With mine supply deficits projected at 8 million tonnes for copper through 2027 (per Wood Mackenzie), we're investing $200 million in battery tech R&D and a new Querétaro, Mexico, assembly line for electric underground equipment, targeting 25% market share in OEM retrofits by 2026.

Agriculture (18% of Q3 revenue, flat YoY): Ag demand cooled sequentially due to normalizing farm incomes—U.S. net farm income dipped 5% to $128 billion per USDA—but replacement cycles and precision ag adoption are supportive. Large tractor orders (over 200 HP), like our 8R series with StarFire autonomy, rose 7% globally, driven by high-crop yields in Brazil's soy belt.

North America (45% of ag exposure) saw 3% growth despite Midwest drought recovery lags, with sprayer attachments up 12% on sustainable farming mandates. South America exploded 15% on record corn/soy harvests—Argentina's planting up 10%—where our autonomous MFWD tractors captured share from John Deere in no-till applications. EMEA was soft at -2%, hit by Ukraine supply disruptions and EU subsidy shifts. Our play: Telematics penetration hit 65% of fleets, enabling predictive maintenance that cuts downtime 18%; we're rolling out NextSwath end-of-row turning on 20 new models, boosting efficiency 10%. A $100 million precision ag center in Iowa positions us for 2025's rebound as input costs ease.

Manufacturing (12% of Q3 revenue, up 11% YoY): Reshoring and automation are the story, with U.S. factory IP up 4.5% per ISM data fueling demand for our forklifts, telehandlers, and material handling systems. Electric counterbalance trucks, like our GP50N with lithium-ion packs, surged 25% in orders, compliant with California's ZEV mandates and Amazon's warehouse electrification.

Asia-Pacific leads at 20% growth on China's "Made in China 2025" fab expansions—our pallet jacks with AI vision are up 30% in EV battery plants. Europe grew 8% on battery gigafactory builds by Northvolt, while North America added 10% from onshoring in semiconductors. Strategically, our $80 million acquisition of a German AGV firm enhances our connected warehouse solutions, targeting 15% EBITDA margins in this high-growth segment. Integration of IoT sensors across 40% of lifts delivers 12% utilization uplift for customers like DHL.

Wrapping up these trends: Across markets, we're navigating macro caution with backlog strength—92% book-to-bill—and margin-accretive aftermarket growth at 16% YoY from parts digitization. Electrification now 22% of orders positions us ahead of Cummins and Volvo in the shift to Tier 4 Final/Stage V equivalents. Regionally, North America and LatAm are our growth engines at 13% combined, offsetting APAC volatility. We're confident in delivering 10-12% organic growth in FY24, supported by $500 million in capex for capacity and tech.

Before we open for questions, I'd like to provide a detailed update on our share repurchase program, which remains a cornerstone of our disciplined capital allocation framework in this cyclical industrial equipment sector.

As you recall, in February 2023, our Board authorized a $2.0 billion open-market share repurchase program, superseding the prior $1.2 billion authorization from 2021 that we fully executed by year-end 2022. This program underscores our confidence in GIDC's long-term value creation potential, particularly as we navigate the post-pandemic recovery in global capex cycles for heavy machinery, earthmoving equipment, and automation systems. We're funding repurchases opportunistically from our robust free cash flow generation—$1.8 billion year-to-date through Q3, up 22% year-over-year—prioritizing buybacks alongside our 2.8% dividend yield and selective M&A, like our recent tuck-in acquisition of a precision CNC machining firm in Germany.

Execution to date has been strong and methodical. Through September 30th, we've repurchased approximately 18.7 million shares, or 4.2% of our diluted shares outstanding, for a total of $1.45 billion. This includes $450 million deployed in Q3 alone, at an average price of $77.50 per share—well below our current trading level around $92 and our estimated intrinsic value north of $110 based on DCF models incorporating 8-10% organic revenue CAGR through 2028.

Breaking it down by quarter for transparency: Q1 2023: $250 million (3.2 million shares, avg. $78.10)—we ramped up post-authorization amid a temporary pullback in industrial production indices. Q2 2023: $320 million (4.1 million shares, avg. $78.05)—capitalizing on seasonal weakness in ag equipment demand. H1 2024: $430 million (5.5 million shares, avg. $78.20)—steady execution despite steel tariff headwinds. Q3 2024: $450 million (5.9 million shares, avg. $76.30)—accelerated purchases during the August dip triggered by broader market concerns over China slowdowns impacting our APAC mining equipment backlog.

We've utilized a mix of execution strategies to minimize market impact and maximize value. About 60% has been through open-market transactions managed under our Rule 10b5-1 plan, which automates purchases during pre-defined trading windows to avoid insider trading perceptions. The remainder includes two opportunistic accelerated share repurchase agreements: a $200 million ASR in Q4 2023 with a major bank, settling at a volume-weighted average price discount, and a $150 million ASR in Q2 2024. This blend has delivered approximately 250 basis points of EPS accretion in FY 2023 and an expected 180 bps in FY 2024, helping offset margin pressure from raw material inflation in our hydraulic systems and powertrain segments.

Regionally, our repurchase capacity is bolstered by divergent cash flow trends. North America contributed 55% of YTD FCF, driven by a 15% surge in aftermarket parts revenue for construction dozers and excavators amid U.S. infrastructure spending under the IIJA. EMEA added 30%, with strength in wind turbine erection cranes and factory automation lines despite energy transition capex delays in Germany. APAC lagged at 15%, reflecting softer demand for underground mining loaders in Australia and China, where industrial robot orders dipped 8% YoY per IFR data—hence our conservative repurchase pace there, focusing instead on inventory optimization.

Strategically, this program aligns with our industry positioning. In manufacturing and industrial equipment, where ROIC hurdles are 12-15% for peers like Caterpillar, Deere, and Ingersoll Rand, repurchases accretively shrink our share count while our book value per share has grown 18% to $42.50. We're enhancing shareholder returns without compromising $1.2 billion in planned FY 2024 capex for next-gen electrification platforms—think our new 500 kW electric wheel loaders debuting in 2025, targeting the EU's net-zero mandates and U.S. IRA incentives. With $550 million remaining under authorization and $2.1 billion in cash equivalents, we have ample dry powder; expect continued opportunistic deployment through 2025, potentially extending the program if FCF exceeds our $2.4 billion guide, barring a severe downturn in global PMI below 48.

This disciplined approach has delivered total shareholder returns of 28% YTD, outpacing the XLI Industrial Select Sector SPDR by 12 points. We're committed to maximizing value in this capital-intensive sector.

Now, I will hand over to David, COO, for an operational update.

David Patel (COO):
Thank you, Lisa. Operationally, we've been focused on streamlining our supply chain and improving manufacturing efficiency. We have implemented several new initiatives that are already yielding positive results, including expansions at key facilities like Peoria, Belo Horizonte, Rockford, and Pune to address capacity constraints and reduce lead times. We are closely monitoring the global supply chain situation—steel and aluminum costs have moderated, but we're hedged through long-term agreements—and taking proactive steps to mitigate any potential disruptions. We are also investing in automation and digital technologies, such as AI-driven predictive maintenance and IoT platforms like TitanConnect and SiteConnect, to enhance our operational capabilities and drive utilization above 92% across our global plants.

Operator:
Thank you. We will now begin the question-and-answer session. Our first question comes from John Ramirez with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

John Ramirez (Goldman Sachs):
Good morning. Can you discuss the impact of rising raw material costs on your profitability?

Lisa Chen:
Thanks for the question, John. We've managed raw material inflation effectively through a combination of pricing discipline and supply chain optimizations. Steel and aluminum input costs peaked at 25% above pre-pandemic levels last year but have moderated 15% sequentially due to our long-term offtake agreements with suppliers like Nucor and Alcoa. Our ForgeForward lean program and just-in-time inventory via SAP S/4HANA have reduced working capital days and unplanned downtime by 22%, generating $80 million in annualized savings. Mid-single-digit price increases on 85% of our portfolio, with 95% acceptance, have more than offset any residual pressures, contributing 300 basis points to margins. Labor inflation at 4.5% is monitored closely, but our $3.8 billion backlog and 70% Q4 visibility give us confidence in our 19-20% Q4 operating margin guide.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Emily Carter with JPMorgan. Please go ahead.

Emily Carter (JPMorgan):
What is your outlook for demand in the aftermarket services business?

Mark Reynolds:
Great question, Emily. Our aftermarket outlook remains very strong, with Q3 revenue hitting $728 million, up 18% YoY and now 36% of total revenue—the highest ever. This high-margin segment, at 48% EBITDA, benefits from an installed base of 150,000 machines and 20+ year lifecycles. Drivers include 82% global capex utilization boosting parts wear, TitanConnect IoT adoption at 27% driving 35% digital upsells, and RemanForge generating $85 million at 55%+ margins. Regionally, North America up 25% on IIJA, APAC 22% on reshoring. We're targeting 40%+ mix by 2025 via M&A like ForgeTech, digital twins with NVIDIA, and outcome-based contracts piloted with Ford. Book-to-bill at 1.25x signals multi-year growth in a $120 billion TAM expanding at 7-9% CAGR.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Mike Lawson with Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

Mike Lawson (Morgan Stanley):
Can you provide an update on your progress in reducing lead times?

David Patel:
Absolutely, Mike. Lead times for core products like our mining haul trucks and excavators are at 9-12 months, stretched due to strong demand and capacity ramps, but we're making solid progress. Our $450 million CapEx this year targets expansions in Peoria, Belo Horizonte, Querétaro, and Pune, boosting output for earthmovers, electric loaders, and CNC systems. Digital tools like SiteConnect on 250,000 assets and AI predictive maintenance have improved factory utilization to 92% and reduced downtime 22-28%. In construction, book-to-bill at 1.35x reflects IIJA tailwinds; mining at 1.15x with autonomous pilots; ag stabilizing at 1.05x. Expect sequential improvements into 2024 as new lines come online, supporting Q4 intake of $2.9-3.1 billion.

Operator:
Thank you. That concludes our Q&A session.

Mark Reynolds:
Thank you for your questions and your interest in Global Industrial Dynamics Corp. We are pleased with our progress this quarter and remain focused on executing our strategy and delivering long-term value for our shareholders.

Sarah Thompson:
Thank you, everyone, for joining us today. This concludes our earnings call. Have a great day.

Operator:
This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for participating. You may now disconnect.
